newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Dollar steady over 1.79 marks despite Waigel.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dollar steady over 1.79 marks despite Waigel.

text.p: The dollar traded firmly above 1.79 marks on Tuesday, more than recovering morning losses prompted by a German minister's suggestion that the U.S. currency's soaring rate was a market overreaction.
Sterling, too, bounced back from a temporary two-pfennig blip caused by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's comment and his insistence that Bonn wanted a strong mark.
The UK's FTSE stock index powered to new high ground around 4,900 points by midday, led by lively banking stocks, but other European bourses were mixed.
At 1130 GMT the dollar was quoted at 1.7960 marks compared with 1.7927 in late trade on Monday, while the pound surged to 3.0270 marks, above its 3.0237 six-year high on Monday.
Waigel said Germany stood by previous agreements on foreign exchange rates within the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations.
"We are interested in a strong deutschemark," Waigel said, adding "We are in contact with our partners."
He was speaking at a news conference in Berlin during a visit to the city of the leadership of his Christian Social Union (CSU) party.
Asked about the strength of the pound and the dollar, Waigel said "I think what's happening at the moment is an overreaction of the markets."
The dollar has lingered near six-year peaks against the mark and the pound hit the highest level since October 1990 against the mark on Monday, raising the spectre of intervention from central banks.
"I wouldn't be surprised if the G7 were considering ways and means of stabilising currencies," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International in London.
But he said a scattergun approach to intervention at a few targeted currencies would probably be the first sign of protest.

Eisuke Sakakibara, Japan's newly appointed vice finance minister for international affairs, was quoted as saying the forex market has excessive expectations of the yen's appreciation, and Japan's trade surplus will not put upward pressure on the yen.
The UK's leading FTSE 100 index, which climbed to a record close on Monday, surged 0.8 percent to touch a new peak of 4,900 points on renewed interest in bank stocks.

"This market still wants to go higher," said the head of market-making at one leading brokerage. "There is a lot of liquidity looking for a solid safe home." The previous all-time high set on July 4 was 4,879.
U.S. shares were mixed in London in thin trading as investors awaited U.S. sales figures and a slew of corporate results, dealers said.
"Trading is spotty, but it feels like the market is ready to consolidate a bit more," said one London dealer.
European investors were awaiting the 1230 GMT release of June retail sales data. The report is expected to show sales rose 0.2 percent last month.

German shares stumbled along in midday dealings as the DAX index showed minor losses. Traders said the market had been hit by some bouts of profit-taking despite the dollar showing renewed strength as it battled towards 1.7950 marks. Chemical shares, particularly Hoechst, were in favour. CURRENCIES AT 1130 GMT
The dollar was at 114.45 yen and 1.7945 marks compared with 113.88 yen and 1.7927 marks in late trading on Monday. STOCK MARKETS AT 1000 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was at 4,900.6, up 43.2 points.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 7.28 points at 4,116.74.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 3.61 at 2,945.20. PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $319.00 compared to the London close of $320.85.
Silver was at $4.26, down four cents from Monday's close.
